chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Small-Cap Integrator at the Center of the AI Buildout

TSS, Inc. (NASDAQ: TSSI), headquartered in ~~Round Rock~~ ==Georgetown==, Texas, sits at an unusual intersection in the AI infrastructure stack: it neither designs silicon nor operates data centers, but performs the precision rack-level assembly work that connects NVIDIA GPU servers to hyperscaler floors. Under President and Chief Executive Officer Darryll Dewan, the company has ridden that positioning through one of the most compressed revenue inflections in its history, converting a legacy data-center-services business into a structural AI rack integration provider across two fiscal years.

The company operates three reportable segments. **Procurement** sources and resells information technology and data-center hardware to enterprise and government customers. **Systems Integration** — the AI-driven growth engine — handles rack-level configuration, burn-in, cabling, and deployment of server systems, increasingly NVIDIA-based GPU racks destined for hyperscaler programs. **Facilities** designs, delivers, and manages modular data-center products for customers requiring deployable on-premises capacity, a slower-growth but recurring-revenue complement to the integration work.

## The Revenue Inflection: 2024–2025

Fiscal 2024 marked the beginning of a step-change as TSS's primary OEM customer — a US-based IT hardware manufacturer that, by the company's own 10-K disclosure, accounted for 99% of revenues in both 2024 and 2025 — began ramping NVIDIA GPU server programs to satisfy hyperscaler demand. Full-year 2024 revenue reached approximately $148.1 million, already a substantial departure from the company's prior run-rate. Fiscal 2025 extended that trajectory: TSS reported total revenue of **$245.7 million**, a 66% year-over-year advance, with net income of $15.1 million (up 153%) and diluted EPS of $0.56 (up 133%). [Full-year 2025 results, TSS IR via StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-k1c2lrh4twml.html)

| Segment | FY 2025 Revenue | FY 2024 Revenue | YoY |
|---|---|---|---|
| Procurement | $197.5M | $117.5M | +68% |
| Systems Integration | $40.3M | $22.6M | +78% |
| Facilities | $7.9M | $8.0M | –1% |
| **Total** | **$245.7M** | **$148.1M** | **+66%** |

Adjusted EBITDA reached $18.6 million for the full year, up 83%, reflecting operating leverage on the high-volume integration work. The fourth quarter alone contributed $60.9 million in revenue — up 22% over the prior-year period — as the newly operational Georgetown facility absorbed expanded rack volumes.

## Georgetown: Scaling the Integration Factory

The capacity story behind the 2025 ramp is inseparable from the Georgetown, Texas facility. TSS signed a ten-year lease (May 2025 through May 2035) for 212,793 square feet at Georgetown Logistics Park, more than doubling the company's prior footprint. The site is engineered specifically for high-power AI rack integration, with 15 megawatts of committed electrical capacity and infrastructure for both air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled racks — the thermal requirements of NVIDIA's current and next-generation GPU server platforms. Total capital investment in the facility is approximately $40 million, funded in part through a $20 million credit facility secured to meet accelerating demand. [Georgetown facility details, StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-inc-signs-long-term-lease-for-larger-factory-to-support-a0gr0oxt49yd.html)

Partial operations at Georgetown began in May 2025; full migration from the prior facility was completed by August 2025. The transition imposed a transitory drag on Q3 2025 — revenue fell to $41.9 million against $70.1 million in the year-ago period as facility costs and ramp inefficiencies suppressed results — before the fourth quarter confirmed the facility's throughput capability.

> "The step-up in Q4 gives us confidence that the structural investments we've made in capacity, systems and talent can scale," Dewan said on the Q4 2025 earnings call. "AI demand is not slowing. Hyperscalers and large enterprises continue to invest in accelerated computing."

In December 2025, TSS extended its long-term AI rack integration agreement with its primary OEM customer for an additional two years, effective November 1, 2025, providing forward revenue visibility through the 2026–2027 window.

## Into 2026: Momentum and Concentration

At the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, TSSI shares traded near $12 — inside a 52-week range of $6.87 to $31.94 — with a market capitalization of approximately $337 million. The compression from the 52-week high reflects both post-ramp multiple contraction and investor scrutiny of customer concentration; the company's 99% single-OEM revenue dependency is among the most acute in the small-cap technology services universe. [TSSI stock data, Stock Analysis](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/tssi/)

First-quarter 2026 results reported in May showed total revenue of $55.3 million — optically down 44% from Q1 2025's anomalously elevated $99 million driven by a procurement surge, but Systems Integration revenue of $14.1 million was up 88% year-over-year, signalling genuine integration volume growth independent of the procurement swing. Management guided full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $20–$22 million, targeting the high end of that range.

> "Demand for AI infrastructure remains at an all-time high and is showing no signs of abating," Dewan told analysts on the Q1 2026 call, adding that within May 2026 the company expected to complete more AI rack integrations than it delivered across all of calendar 2025.

A second facility — the former Round Rock headquarters — was converted in May 2026 to serve as dedicated AI rack materials warehousing for the primary OEM customer, extending the integration logistics footprint. Capital expenditure of $17 million was planned through the third quarter of 2026 to support next-generation rack architectures.

## What the Dossier Asks

This dossier examines the five questions that will determine TSS's trajectory through 2028: whether AI rack integration revenue can sustain and diversify beyond its current single-OEM concentration; how the Georgetown facility's expanded capacity translates into throughput economics as GPU rack architectures evolve toward liquid cooling and higher power density; whether the Facilities segment's modular data-center product line can find a second growth vector in the AI-adjacent on-premises market; how management executes the ongoing capital-expenditure cycle without straining the balance sheet; and whether a small-cap integrator with limited analyst coverage and high beta exposure can hold a structural competitive position as OEMs and hyperscalers evaluate insourcing integration work at scale.

---

**Sources:** [StockTitan — FY2025 results](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-k1c2lrh4twml.html) · [StockTitan — Georgetown lease](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-inc-signs-long-term-lease-for-larger-factory-to-support-a0gr0oxt49yd.html) · [StockTitan — 10-K filing summary](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/TSSI/10-k-tss-inc-files-annual-report-11585bc4230e.html) · [StockTitan — Q3 2025 10-Q](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/TSSI/10-q-tss-inc-quarterly-earnings-report-d5a331bbca85.html) · [Stock Analysis — TSSI overview](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/tssi/) · [Daily Political — Q1 2026 call highlights](https://www.dailypolitical.com/2026/05/12/tss-q1-earnings-call-highlights.html) · [Minichart — FY2025 results summary](https://www.minichart.com.sg/2026/03/11/tss-inc-achieves-record-2025-results-with-66-revenue-growth-and-strong-ai-integration-outlook-for-2026/)

chapters.title: From legacy data-center-services through the AI rack integration inflection
chapters.body:
## From Fortress to TSS: A Company Remade in Round Rock

The lineage of TSS, Inc. begins not with AI infrastructure but with concrete and conduit. Incorporated in Delaware in December 2004 as Fortress International Group, Inc., the company spent its first decade as a provider of consulting, engineering, construction management, and facilities services for mission-critical data centers — the unglamorous work of erecting and maintaining physical plant. Anthony Angelini, who served as chief executive for approximately eleven years, built a business tethered to the traditional enterprise data-center cycle: capacity planning, facility build-outs, on-site management contracts.

The pivot came in May 2013. Fortress acquired the data center integration services business of arvato digital services LLC, headquartered in Round Rock, Texas, for roughly $1.5 million in cash. The arvato unit was performing custom rack layout design, configuration, assembly, and deployment of enterprise IT infrastructure — server banks, storage, networking, structured cabling, power, and cooling — for large enterprise customers. It brought with it eleven employees, an annualised revenue run-rate the company described as exceeding $10 million, and, crucially, an operational address nine miles from Dell Technologies' global headquarters. On June 7, 2013, shareholders approved a corporate name change to TSS, Inc. — Total Site Solutions — and trading on the OTCQB marketplace under the symbol TSSI commenced three days later. The rebrand was, as Angelini signalled at the time, a declaration of intent: legacy construction-and-maintenance work would be subordinated to a technology-services identity anchored in rack integration.

## Modular Data Centers and the Facilities Foundation

The Facilities segment that TSS inherited from the Fortress years provided another architectural pillar. Modular data centers — prefabricated, deployable units that enterprises and government agencies could position at edge locations or use as overflow capacity without large construction programmes — carried economics the rest of the business could not easily replicate. Gross margins on MDC service contracts ran between fifty and sixty-five percent, against the low single digits available in hardware reselling. By the mid-2010s TSS had integrated more than 500 modular data centers and maintained more than 100 under active service agreements.

The MDC segment served a diversified customer base across enterprise, financial services, and government. It supplied Dewan and his predecessors with a recurring-revenue base that cushioned the lumpier procurement and integration lines. That cushion came, however, with an inherent limitation: modular data center retirements were outpacing new deployments by the early 2020s, and the segment entered gentle secular contraction precisely as hyperscaler-driven demand for the AI-rack work was about to accelerate. The high-margin Facilities business would increasingly function as financial ballast rather than growth engine.

## Building the Dell Relationship and Systems Integration Discipline

The strategic anchor that would ultimately define TSS was being forged quietly through the 2010s. The Round Rock address mattered. Dell Technologies' procurement, supply-chain, and integration operations were concentrated in the same geography, and the integration capability TSS acquired from arvato had been performing rack build-outs for Dell-affiliated programmes before the acquisition. By the time TSS launched a formal procurement services line in 2019 — acting as an authorised sourcing intermediary for Dell hardware on behalf of end-customers — the commercial relationship had deepened into something close to structural dependency.

Revenues during this transitional era reflected the latent scale of the Dell channel. From roughly $27 million in fiscal 2021, TSS rebounded to $30.6 million in fiscal 2022, with the Systems Integration segment contributing $7.2 million in pure integration services. The Dell relationship had not yet produced the volume inflection that would come, but it was accumulating strategic mass: certifications, facility familiarity, operational trust. Dell was building a case file on TSS's execution reliability, and TSS was building the integration muscle memory — rack design, configuration, burn-in testing, documentation discipline — that hyperscaler programmes would demand at a different order of magnitude.

## Darryll Dewan and the 2023 Transformation

On November 14, 2022, TSS announced that Darryll Dewan had succeeded Angelini as President and Chief Executive Officer. Dewan brought a thirty-year pedigree in enterprise IT that ran from IBM through i2 Technologies to a decade at Dell Technologies, where he had served as Vice President of Global Sales and Field Marketing. His parting message at the Dell unit — overseeing direct and indirect sales for Dell's endpoint security division — left him unusually well-positioned to understand what hyperscaler customers needed from data-centre integration partners. Board chairman Peter Woodward said Dewan had "created tremendous wealth for investors" in prior roles. Dewan's own framing was more operational: "TSS is well positioned strategically to expand our customer base and capabilities to address a wider market."

The 2023 results validated the framing. Revenue grew seventy-eight percent to $54.4 million. Procurement services — channelling Dell hardware to enterprise end-customers — surged to $38.5 million from $13.2 million. Operating income rose ninety-one percent. The Dell relationship accounted for ninety-six percent of total revenues.

> "2023 was a transformational year for TSS. We grew revenues 78% in 2023 and increased our operating income by 91% compared to 2022. As generative AI, cybersecurity and other advanced computing technologies drive data center demand, TSS is uniquely positioned to capitalize on these trends with our leading-edge system integration and deployment capabilities."
> — Darryll Dewan, FY2023 earnings call, March 28, 2024

Dell formalised the recognition in September 2023, presenting TSS with its [2023 First Choice Partner Award](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2023/09/13/2742884/0/en/TSS-INC-Wins-Dell-Technologies-2023-First-Choice-Partner-Award.html) for performance as a data-centre integration partner.

## The AI Rack Integration Inflection: xAI, Colossus, and the 2024 Breakout

By early 2024, Dewan was describing plans to scale rack integration "up to 10x over 2023 results" within sixty days — a statement that seemed extraordinary against a base of $8.8 million in pure integration services. The catalyst was already in motion. Dell had been selected, alongside Super Micro Computer, to supply the initial tranche of server infrastructure for xAI's Colossus supercluster in Memphis, Tennessee — an ambitious project assembling 100,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs in four months. The Phase 1 build was split between Dell and SMCI. Phase 2, targeting another hundred-thousand-GPU expansion, went entirely to Dell.

TSS had signed on as Dell's designated integration partner for the programme. Production of AI-enabled racks commenced at the Round Rock facility in June 2024, funded in part by $1.7 million in capex reimbursement from Dell. The second quarter of 2024 captured one month of the Phase 1 build-out; the third quarter captured three full months of meaningful volume.

> "Q3 2024 was the first quarter that includes a full period of revenue for AI-enabled server rack integrations at meaningful volumes."
> — Darryll Dewan, Q3 2024 earnings call, November 14, 2024

Systems Integration revenue hit $7.6 million in a single quarter — matching the entire fiscal 2022 annual integration figure in ninety days. For full-year 2024, the Systems Integration segment posted $22.6 million, up 157 percent year-over-year. Total revenue reached [$148.1 million](https://ir.tssiusa.com/tss-revenue-grows-172-to-a-record-148-1-million-in-fy-2024-increases-eps-to-0-24-up-from-0-00-in-2023/), a 172 percent increase. Net income went from $74,000 in 2023 to $6.0 million. Diluted earnings per share moved from zero to $0.24.

In October 2024, TSS and Dell signed a multi-year agreement establishing minimum volume commitments for ongoing AI-enabled rack integration. The same month, TSS announced approval for uplisting to the Nasdaq Capital Market — trading on the exchange began November 14, 2024, the second anniversary of Dewan's appointment.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Systems Integration Revenue | Operating Income |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $30.6M | $7.2M | $0.9M |
| 2023 | $54.4M | ~$8.8M | $1.75M |
| 2024 | $148.1M | $22.6M | ~~$8.5M~~ ==$5.8M== |
| 2025 | $245.7M | $40.3M | ~~—~~ ==$6.3M== |

## Georgetown: Building Capacity for the Next Phase

The October 2024 multi-year agreement made the Round Rock facility's constraints immediately apparent. The site carried roughly 2.7 megawatts of available power against integration programmes that would require an order of magnitude more. On December 5, 2024, TSS [announced a long-term lease](https://ir.tssiusa.com/tss-inc-signs-long-term-lease-for-larger-factory-to-support-accelerating-demand-for-ai-enabled-technologies/) for a 212,793 square-foot facility at Georgetown Logistics Park — more than double the Round Rock footprint — located at 1800 Aviation Drive, ==Suite 100, ==Georgetown, Texas.

> "The new facility more than doubles our square footage and positions TSS to continue our rapid growth."
> — Darryll Dewan, December 2024

The Georgetown site was designed to expand from an initial six megawatts of available power toward fifteen megawatts committed by the City of Georgetown, accommodating both air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled rack integration — the latter essential for next-generation GPU server programmes running at rack densities that air cooling cannot address. Leasehold improvements were projected at approximately $35.1 million, financed partly through a construction loan from Susser Bank of up to $20 million. Production began at Georgetown on May 7, 2025; full migration from Round Rock completed in August of that year, with the old facility retained for warehousing AI rack material. Dewan told investors the Georgetown site would enable "several times" more rack integrations per period than Round Rock had allowed.

Fiscal 2025 extended the trajectory: revenue reached $245.7 million, Systems Integration grew another seventy-eight percent to $40.3 million, net income rose to $15.1 million, and the headcount doubled to 286 full-time employees. What had been a $30 million data-center-services company in 2022 had, in thirty-six months, become a quarter-billion-dollar AI infrastructure integrator — still concentrated in a single OEM relationship, but running at a scale that would have been unrecognisable to the Fortress International Group that broke ground on its first mission-critical facility two decades earlier.

chapters.title: Procurement, Systems Integration, Facilities — the three-segment structure
chapters.body:
TSS operates through three discrete reporting segments — Procurement, Systems Integration, and Facilities — whose revenue trajectories diverged sharply across the 2023-to-2025 AI infrastructure buildout. The architecture was in place before the inflection, but it was the sudden acceleration of Systems Integration volume that reset how investors and customers alike understood what the company actually does.

## Procurement: Volume Machine, Thin Spread

The Procurement segment sources IT and data center hardware — servers, networking equipment, storage, peripherals — on behalf of enterprise and hyperscaler customers. TSS acts as an intermediary, taking title to goods and reselling them, which means segment revenues are reported gross: the full invoice value of hardware flows through the income statement, compressing the apparent margin considerably.

The growth numbers are striking. Procurement revenue stood at roughly $38.5 million in fiscal 2023. It jumped to $117.5 million in fiscal 2024 — a 205 percent increase — before reaching $197.5 million in fiscal 2025, another 68 percent gain. Over the same two years, the segment went from a rounding error at a $30 million company to the single largest revenue line by a wide margin, representing about 80 percent of total revenue across the cycle.

Dewan flagged the structural reality plainly in early 2025:

> "Procurement Services represents nearly 80% of revenues in 2024 and is characterized by wider quarter-to-quarter revenue variability and margins that are typically below our corporate average."

The gross margin on Procurement is mechanically suppressed by the gross-revenue recognition method. On a GAAP basis the segment ran at roughly 6 to 8 percent gross margin across 2024-2025. The practical economics are narrower: TSS earns a spread on hardware sourcing that, on a non-GAAP basis, reflected a 4 to 5 percent margin on the spread rather than the full invoice value. Within that constraint, Procurement still contributed meaningful operating income — the Q3 2025 segment disclosure showed $31.1 million of revenue generating $2.6 million of gross profit and $1.9 million of operating income, a thin-but-positive contribution that scales with volume.

The volatility is real. Quarterly Procurement revenue ranged from $4.9 million in Q2 2024 to $90.2 million in Q1 2025 — an eighteen-fold swing — depending on customer purchasing cycles and hardware availability. That lumpiness is structural, not exceptional.

## Systems Integration: The Margin and Growth Engine

Systems Integration is where TSS's strategic value is concentrated. The segment encompasses rack-level configuration, component installation, firmware loading, burn-in testing, and pre-deployment validation of complete server systems — with AI GPU racks, specifically NVIDIA-based compute nodes destined for hyperscaler data centers, as the primary workload since 2023.

The segment's numbers tell the inflection story cleanly. Revenue was $8.8 million in fiscal 2023. It more than doubled to $22.6 million in fiscal 2024 and nearly doubled again to $40.3 million in fiscal 2025. Then in Q1 2026 — the most recent quarter within the frozen window — Systems Integration posted $14.1 million, up 88 percent year-over-year from the $7.5 million recorded in Q1 2025.

| Fiscal Year | SI Revenue | SI Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $8.8M | ~20–25% |
| FY2024 | $22.6M | ~30–44% (quarterly range) |
| FY2025 | $40.3M | ~~—~~ ==~30.9%== |
| Q1 2026 | $14.1M | 37.5% |

The margin profile is structurally different from Procurement. Systems Integration gross margins ranged from roughly 22 percent to 44 percent in individual quarters through 2024-2025, reflecting the labor and facility intensity of the work and the pricing premium that complex AI rack integration commands. At Q1 2026, the segment ran at 37.5 percent gross margin on $14.1 million of revenue, producing $5.3 million of gross profit — the highest absolute gross profit in the segment's history to that point, and materially higher than the $1.7 million the same quarter generated one year earlier.

Dewan, reporting third-quarter 2024 results as the first quarter that included "a full period of revenue for AI-enabled server rack integrations at meaningful volumes," framed the scale shift directly:

> "In the third quarter, procurement revenues alone exceeded the entire company's total revenues for all of 2023."

He added, anticipating the multi-year trajectory:

> "Even more encouraging is the recent signing of an agreement with one of our largest customers to build similar volumes of AI-enabled racks for the next several years."

That agreement, later extended in December 2025 by two additional years, is the structural anchor of the Systems Integration business. The segment's operating leverage story runs through fixed facility costs and labor efficiency: as rack volumes rise within a given facility footprint, incremental revenue falls largely to gross profit with limited marginal cost growth. The Georgetown expansion — 212,793 square feet of light industrial space, roughly $40 million in facility improvements, lease running through May 2035 — was built explicitly to capture that leverage at larger scale.

> "At full capacity, this new facility enables us to integrate several times the number of data center racks we can currently integrate."

Q3 2025 briefly interrupted the narrative. The Systems Integration segment generated only $9.2 million of revenue in that quarter — below the pace needed to hit annual targets — and posted a segment operating loss of $703,000 as fixed costs at the new Georgetown facility ran ahead of volume. Dewan attributed the miss to "unforeseen operational requirements" in the transition: power infrastructure upgrades, ERP migration, and expanded staffing requirements all compressed throughput simultaneously. By Q4 2025, the company reported that rack volumes had recovered sharply, and the full-year Systems Integration total of $40.3 million reflected the disruption only partially.

## Facilities: High-Margin Anchor, Small Scale

The Facilities segment encompasses two distinct offerings: modular data center products — deployable, pre-configured data center units sold to enterprise and government customers that need on-premises computing capacity outside traditional colocation environments — and on-site facility management services, under which TSS provides ongoing operations and maintenance for customer-owned data center infrastructure.

Revenue in this segment has been stable rather than growing. The segment generated $7.1 million in fiscal 2023, $8.0 million in fiscal 2024, and $7.9 million in fiscal 2025. Quarterly revenues have run between $1.3 million and $2.0 million throughout the 2024-2025 period. The Q3 2025 10-Q reported $1.6 million of segment revenue generating $881,000 of gross profit — a 55 percent gross margin — and $729,000 of segment operating income.

That margin profile is the defining feature. Facilities gross margins have consistently run in the 55 to 74 percent range across quarters, and the fiscal 2025 10-K noted that "Facilities management margins remained high near 60%, but that segment is small." The management services component — recurring, contract-based, and largely non-cyclical — provides a stable baseline that partially offsets the lumpiness in Procurement and the capital-intensity ramp in Systems Integration.

The modular data center product line has attracted less attention than the AI integration business, but it addresses a real structural gap: enterprises and government agencies that cannot wait for colocation capacity, cannot expose sensitive workloads to shared infrastructure, or operate in geographies where hyperscaler regions are absent. TSS's product capability here positions it alongside specialized providers of containerized and modular data center solutions, a market that has seen renewed interest as government AI initiatives and defense edge-computing programs have expanded.

## Segment Mix and the Operating Leverage Curve

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q1 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Procurement | $38.5M | $117.5M | $197.5M | $40.0M |
| Systems Integration | $8.8M | $22.6M | $40.3M | $14.1M |
| Facilities | $7.1M | $8.0M | $7.9M | $1.3M |
| **Total** | **$54.4M** | **$148.1M** | **$245.7M** | **$55.3M** |

The consolidated picture shows a company whose revenue tripled across two years primarily on Procurement volume while Systems Integration — the higher-margin, strategically differentiated segment — scaled in parallel. The blended gross margin fell from 20.2 percent in fiscal 2023 to 15.1 percent in fiscal 2024 and 13.2 percent in fiscal 2025 as the mix shifted toward lower-margin Procurement. But absolute gross profit expanded from $11.0 million to $22.4 million to $32.4 million over the same span, and adjusted EBITDA rose from roughly $2.7 million to $10.2 million to $18.6 million — a compound that reflects operating leverage rather than margin erosion.

Dewan's framing of the dynamics at the mid-2025 mark was precise:

> "Total revenue for the first half of 2025 exceeded total revenue in the second half of 2024. These results reflect strong operational execution and the growing leverage in our business model."

The leverage resides primarily in Systems Integration: Georgetown's fixed cost base — lease, power infrastructure, integration equipment, workforce — is largely sunk once the facility is operational. Each additional rack integrated against that base carries high incremental margin. As of Q1 2026, with the facility "running at increasing scale for six months" in Dewan's words, the segment's margin recovery toward the 37 to 44 percent gross margin band was the clearest signal that the operating model was performing as designed.

The customer concentration that underpins all three segments — a single marquee OEM partner representing ~~99 percent of total revenue across fiscal 2023, 2024, and 2025~~ ==approximately 96 percent of total revenue in fiscal 2023 and approximately 99 percent in both fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025== — is the structural condition within which this leverage plays out. The [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TSSI&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10) states plainly that a reduction in volume from that customer "could have a disproportionate negative effect on operating results." The December 2025 contract extension was, among other things, the company's answer to that risk: two additional years of contracted volume against a facility built to deliver it.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment economics, operating leverage, capital structure
chapters.body:
## From Narrow Base to Nine-Figure Scale

For most of its operating life, TSS, Inc. generated revenue that measured in the tens of millions and rarely compelled a second glance. In fiscal 2022, the ~~Round Rock~~ ==Georgetown==, Texas company posted $30.6 million in total revenue — a modest 11.8 per cent advance over the prior year, adequate to keep the lights on at its modular data-centre and IT-procurement businesses but nothing that suggested the company was standing at the threshold of a structural step-change. Two fiscal years later, that same company reported $148.1 million — a 172 per cent increase over 2023 — and by the end of fiscal 2025 had eclipsed $245 million. The driver, in each successive year, was an escalating volume of AI rack integration work tied to the global hyperscaler buildout.

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue | YoY Growth | Adjusted EBITDA | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $30.6M | +11.8% | $1.7M | 5.5% |
| FY2023 | $54.4M | +77.6% | $2.7M | 4.9% |
| FY2024 | $148.1M | +172.3% | $10.2M | 6.9% |
| FY2025 | $245.7M | +65.9% | $18.6M | 7.6% |

*Sources: [TSSI FY2024 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1320760/000165495425004295/tssi_10k.htm); [FY2024 earnings release, TSS IR](https://investors.tssiusa.com); FY2025 annual results, March 2026*

The trajectory is striking not merely for its slope but for the inflection that preceded it. Fiscal 2023 was, in the words of Darryll Dewan on the subsequent earnings call, "a transformational year for TSS," one in which revenues grew 78 per cent and operating income advanced 91 per cent. But the more consequential signal came at year-end, when the company disclosed that its marquee OEM customer — an unnamed US-based IT original equipment manufacturer — had begun ramping AI server deployments. Dewan told investors in March 2024 that TSS had "modelled plans to scale our data centre rack integration business up to 10x over our 2023 rack integration results," adding that the company expected "to benefit from this growth beginning in the second half of this year, 2024." The forecast proved conservative.

## Segment Economics: A Revenue Mix Story

TSS reports across three operating segments whose economic characteristics diverge substantially, a structure that makes headline revenue an imprecise guide to value creation. The Procurement segment — sourcing and reselling servers, networking equipment, and data-centre hardware to enterprise and government customers — generates the largest revenue volumes but at thin margins of roughly six to seven cents on the dollar. Systems Integration, which performs rack-level configuration, burn-in testing, and deployment of GPU-dense AI server systems, commands gross margins in the 22-to-32 per cent range and in recent quarters has approached 37-38 per cent as throughput per technician improved at the Georgetown facility. Facilities — encompassing modular data-centre products and on-site facility management — has historically produced the highest segment margins, typically in the 55-to-62 per cent range, but remains a comparatively small contributor by absolute revenue.

| Segment | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Procurement | $13.2M | $38.5M | $117.5M | $197.5M |
| Systems Integration | $7.2M | $8.8M | $22.6M | $40.3M |
| Facilities | $10.2M | $7.1M | $8.0M | $7.9M |
| **Total** | **$30.6M** | **$54.4M** | **$148.1M** | **$245.7M** |

The table illustrates a tension that runs through the financial narrative: it is Procurement, not Systems Integration, that generates the headline revenue swell. In fiscal 2024 Procurement accounted for roughly 79 per cent of group revenue; in fiscal 2025 it had grown to 80 per cent. The segment's growth, however, is intrinsically tied to the same OEM relationship that drives Systems Integration — procurement orders for AI servers essentially flow upstream of the integration work, creating a compounding single-customer exposure that the company discloses consistently in its risk-factor sections.

Systems Integration, meanwhile, grew from $8.8 million in fiscal 2023 to $40.3 million by fiscal 2025, a 358 per cent advance across two years. On a margin-contribution basis, the segment's economics are disproportionate to its revenue share. In the first quarter of 2026, with revenue of $14.1 million, Systems Integration generated a gross margin of approximately 37.5 per cent — a 1,500 basis-point expansion from the equivalent period a year earlier — as Georgetown facility throughput ramped and fixed infrastructure costs were spread across higher unit volumes.

## The Operating Leverage Thesis Playing Out

The EBITDA progression — from $1.7 million in fiscal 2022 to $18.6 million in fiscal 2025 — captures the operating leverage dynamic that distinguished TSS from a pure contract integrator. Fixed costs associated with maintaining a certified integration facility, retaining technicians, and administering the OEM programme agreements do not scale linearly with rack volume. As integration throughput increased, the cost base that was in place from early in the ramp continued to absorb a shrinking fraction of incremental revenue.

Gross profit accordingly moved from $9.0 million in fiscal 2022 to $32.4 million in fiscal 2025, a 261 per cent advance against a 702 per cent revenue increase over the same span — a compression in blended gross margins (from 29.3 per cent in 2022 to 13.2 per cent in 2025) that reflected Procurement's growing share, while the underlying Integration margins held firm or improved.

The operating income line followed a less linear path, revealing the capital commitment required to support the Georgetown build. The company recorded operating income of $5.8 million in fiscal 2024 and ~~an equivalent figure~~ ==$6.3 million== in fiscal 2025, but the quarterly distribution within fiscal 2025 was pronounced: operating income of $4.1 million in the first quarter was followed by a loss of $931,000 in the third quarter as facility ramp costs — lease expenses, fit-out, power infrastructure — loaded into results before full throughput had been established. Dewan acknowledged the dynamic in the company's third-quarter 2025 commentary, noting that year-to-date revenue growth of 88 per cent and adjusted EBITDA improvement of 59 per cent "underscore the strength and momentum of our business" even as short-term costs temporarily clouded the operating line.

> "We are pleased to have surpassed the upper end of our outlook for 2025. Systems integration rack volumes at our new Georgetown facility came online mid-year and ramped in the fourth quarter, positioning the company for solid growth in 2026." — Darryll Dewan, March 2026

Net income for fiscal 2025 was reported at $15.1 million, though the headline required a footnote: the figure included a $7.6 million non-cash benefit from the release of a deferred tax asset valuation allowance — a technical recognition that TSS had established sufficient earnings history to justify carrying forward the tax asset. Stripping that benefit, underlying operational net income was approximately $7.5 million, representing a diluted EPS of roughly $0.28 versus the reported $0.56.

## Capital Structure and the Georgetown Commitment

TSS entered the AI ramp with a lean balance sheet that was simultaneously its most manageable characteristic and its binding constraint. Cash at the end of fiscal 2023 stood at $11.8 million against total assets of $25.6 million and debt of $4.3 million. The company had modest leverage, modest equity, and a workforce scaled for a $50 million revenue business.

The Georgetown facility commitment, announced and executed through 2024 and into 2025, required a meaningful escalation of capital deployment. The company signed a ten-year lease at Georgetown Logistics Park in Georgetown, Texas, covering 212,793 square feet — a facility designed to support a power draw expansion from an initial 2.7 megawatts to 15 megawatts operational, with infrastructure plans targeting 40-plus megawatts. Capital expenditure associated with the build reached approximately $32.7 million in fiscal 2025.

To support that commitment, TSS drew a $20 million term loan from Susser Bank in the second quarter of 2025, priced at one-month SOFR plus 300 basis points with a 4.5 per cent floor, maturing January 2030. A $5 million accordion draw followed in September 2025. The company factored receivables to accelerate working capital conversion; gross factored volumes for the nine months ending September 2025 reached $259.4 million, with fees of $3.3 million — a cost that reflects the liquidity management demands of a business operating at 99 per cent customer concentration with chunky invoice cycles.

The equity capital structure was substantively reset in August 2025, when TSS completed a public offering that raised $55.3 million net from the issuance of 3.45 million new shares. The proceeds effectively recapitalised the balance sheet: cash at year-end 2025 reached $85.5 million against total debt of $41.6 million (including operating leases), and stockholders' equity advanced from $7.1 million at year-end 2024 to $76.6 million twelve months later — a balance-sheet transformation that reflected both retained earnings and the offering proceeds.

| | YE 2022 | YE 2023 | YE 2024 | YE 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | $20.4M | $11.8M | $23.2M | $85.5M |
| Total Debt | $4.8M | $4.3M | $32.7M | $41.6M |
| Stockholders' Equity | $2.9M | $3.6M | $7.1M | $76.6M |
| Total Assets | $31.4M | $25.6M | $96.6M | $184.9M |

*Source: [SEC EDGAR balance-sheet disclosures, TSSI annual filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TSSI&type=10-K)*

## Customer Concentration: The Structural Caveat

No financial analysis of TSS can omit the single fact that overshadows every revenue line and every margin improvement: one unnamed US-based IT OEM customer accounted for 96 per cent of revenues in fiscal 2023, 99 per cent in fiscal 2024, and 99 per cent again in fiscal 2025. At the end of the first quarter of 2026, that same customer represented 99 per cent of revenues and 88 per cent of accounts receivable.

The company has disclosed this concentration consistently and at length in its 10-K risk factors, making no effort to downplay what it describes as a potential material adverse effect were the relationship to be curtailed, modified, or lost. A long-term AI rack integration agreement signed with the customer in October 2024 — then amended and extended in December 2025 with a two-year term extension, automatic one-year renewals, and minimum monthly payment commitments calibrated to cover facility and debt service — provides contractual visibility. It does not eliminate the concentration.

> "2024 was a transformative year by all accounts, driven by strong operational execution and our commitment to customer service as we capture the soaring demand for AI rack integration and capitalize on opportunistic procurement services." — Darryll Dewan, [FY2024 earnings release, March 27, 2025](https://investors.tssiusa.com)

For fiscal 2026, TSS entered the year with adjusted EBITDA guidance of $20 million to $22 million — a range that Dewan said in May 2026 the company was "tracking toward the high end of." The first quarter delivered $5.3 million in adjusted EBITDA on revenue of $55.4 million, and Dewan stated that within that month the company would have completed more rack integrations than it delivered across all of 2025. The operating leverage thesis was still live; the customer-concentration risk had not, as of the frozen snapshot date, materially changed.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Multiple Compression After the Peak

TSS, Inc. reached a fifty-two-week high of $31.94 before drifting to approximately $12.00 by the frozen-snapshot date of 23 May 2026 — a 62% drawdown that tells the first part of the valuation story. The retreat was not a verdict on deteriorating fundamentals; revenues grew 65.9% year-over-year to $245.7 million in FY2025 and adjusted EBITDA expanded from $10.2 million to $18.6 million. What changed was the risk discount. As investors moved from pricing in unbounded AI ramp extrapolation to pricing in a more sober read of 99% single-customer revenue concentration and a contract horizon capped at November 2027, the multiple contracted sharply.

At $12 per share with approximately 28 million shares outstanding, TSSI carried a market capitalisation of roughly $337 million. Against year-end 2025 balance-sheet figures of $85.5 million in cash and $41.6 million in total debt, enterprise value worked out to approximately $293 million. That baseline drives all the multiples that follow.

## Current Valuation Multiples

The trailing multiple frame rests on FY2025's $18.6 million adjusted EBITDA, $245.7 million in revenue, and approximately $7.5 million in cash net income once the non-recurring $7.6 million deferred tax asset valuation-allowance release is stripped from the reported $15.1 million figure. On those figures:

| Multiple | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| EV / Trailing EBITDA | ~15.8x | $293M EV / $18.6M adj. EBITDA |
| Forward EV / EBITDA | ~14.0x | $293M EV / $21M FY2026 guidance midpoint |
| EV / Trailing Sales | ~1.19x | $293M EV / $245.7M revenue |
| Reported Trailing P/E | ~~22x~~ ==~21x== | ~~$12 / ~$0.54 diluted EPS~~ ==$12 / ~$0.56 diluted EPS== |
| Cash P/E (ex tax benefit) | ~44x | $12 / ~$0.27 underlying EPS |
| Price / Book | ~4.4x | $337M market cap / $76.6M stockholders' equity |

The cash P/E figure of approximately 44 times underlying earnings is the most striking line in the table. It reflects the reality that TSS, while generating meaningful EBITDA, converts a relatively small fraction of that into distributable earnings after depreciation charges on a swiftly growing fixed-asset base — the Georgetown facility alone absorbed $32.7 million in FY2025 capital expenditure, with a further $17 million planned through Q3 2026 — and after interest service on the Susser Bank term loan. The EV/EBITDA band of 14–16x is the market's operative lens; it aligns with how acquirers and comparables-driven investors frame a services business at this margin and growth profile.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

Identifying a tight peer set is complicated by the unusual configuration of TSS's business — a single-customer AI rack integrator that also operates a modular data centre product line and a procurement pass-through. The closest analogs span the contract electronics manufacturing space, the IT distribution and solutions segment, and the broader AI infrastructure services category.

| Company | Ticker | ~Revenue | Trailing EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | Trailing P/E | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSS, Inc. | TSSI | $246M | ~15.8x | ~1.19x | ~~22x~~ ==~21x== (rptd.) | 99% OEM concentration; AI rack ramp |
| Celestica | CLS | ~~$4.5B~~ ==~$9.7B== | ~16x | ~1.1x | ~26x | EMS with strong AI server exposure; closest integration analog |
| Jabil | JBL | ~$28B | ~9x | ~0.4x | ~14x | Large EMS; diversified; lower AI premium |
| Insight Enterprises | NSIT | ~$10B | ~11x | ~0.3x | ~16x | IT solutions and integration; multi-customer |
| ePlus | PLUS | ~$2B | ~9x | ~0.6x | ~14x | Smaller IT solutions integrator |
| TD SYNNEX | SNX | ~$58B | ~9x | ~0.15x | ~13x | IT distribution; thin margin, diversified |

*Peer multiples are approximate estimates based on market data available within the frozen-snapshot window; figures will vary by source and calculation convention.*

Several observations emerge. Celestica — the closest analog on the AI server integration dimension — trades at roughly comparable EV/EBITDA to TSSI, though with materially higher revenue diversification and a customer base spanning multiple hyperscalers. That rough parity suggests the market is not giving TSSI an obvious discount for its AI exposure so much as it is applying a concentration penalty that approximately offsets what might otherwise be a scale-and-growth premium. The traditional IT integrators — Insight Enterprises, ePlus, SYNNEX — trade at a meaningful discount to TSSI on EBITDA multiples, reflecting their more commoditised, lower-margin, and slower-growth profiles. On EV/Sales, TSSI's 1.19x sits above the IT services group but lands near Celestica's 1.1x, a comparison that modestly flatters TSS given its lower absolute margins and more concentrated risk.

## What the Current Price Implies

A reverse-DCF framing makes the market's implicit assumptions explicit. At $293 million in enterprise value and a notional 12% WACC, the current price requires the company to generate roughly $21 million in FY2026 adjusted EBITDA — in line with management guidance — and then sustain 8–10% annual EBITDA growth through approximately FY2030, reaching $31–35 million, before entering a terminal phase at modest low-single-digit growth. In practice, the market is giving TSS credit for the Georgetown ramp delivering as planned and the OEM relationship continuing in some form past the November 2027 contract expiry, but is not ascribing meaningful option value to a second re-rating event, a new marquee customer, or further margin expansion.

Critically, the $85.5 million cash balance — itself the product of the August 2025 equity offering that raised $55.3 million net — creates a partial floor. Stripping net cash from the market capitalisation, TSS's operating business is implicitly valued at roughly $250 million, or approximately 13.5x trailing adjusted EBITDA. For a business running 65% revenue growth with a signed long-term integration agreement, that is a sober number. It prices in the cliff risk.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — Georgetown delivers and contract extends (price target: $20–24 per share).** The scenario requires the OEM customer to follow through on guidance pointing to roughly doubling its AI infrastructure investment in 2026 relative to 2025, that the Georgetown facility achieves target throughput — Dewan told investors in May 2026 that the company expected to complete more AI rack integrations that single month than it had across all of FY2025 — and that the OEM agreement is renewed or extended past November 2027. EBITDA in this scenario reaches $28–34 million by FY2026–2027 on margin expansion toward 11–12% as fixed costs are absorbed and the Systems Integration segment becomes a larger share of the revenue mix. A re-rating to 18–20x EV/EBITDA, reflecting reduced contract-cliff anxiety, would produce an enterprise value of approximately $560–640 million and an equity value in the range of $21–24 per share.

**Base case — guidance executes, trajectory stabilises (price target: $11–14 per share).** FY2026 adjusted EBITDA arrives near the $21 million guidance midpoint. The OEM relationship continues on terms broadly consistent with the current agreement through its stated life. Georgetown capacity supports growth into 2026 but the post-2027 growth rate remains uncertain, constraining multiple expansion. The stock continues to trade at approximately 14x forward EV/EBITDA, with equity value in the $11–14 band. This is where the current price anchors — which is either confirmation that the market has it broadly right or an opportunity cost argument for investors who believe contract extension is more probable than the discount implies.

**Bear case — contract cliff materialises (price target: $4–6 per share).** If the OEM customer internalises rack integration capabilities after the November 2027 agreement lapses, or if hyperscaler AI capital expenditure cycles lower and volume softens, TSSI faces a sharp revenue step-down toward the legacy $50–100 million range. EBITDA would compress to an estimated $6–10 million against a fixed-cost base anchored by the Georgetown facility lease obligation and debt service. At 8–9x EV/EBITDA on a distressed base, enterprise value falls to roughly $60–80 million, yielding equity value after net-debt settlement of approximately $4–6 per share. The Georgetown facility — carrying more than $50 million in accumulated capex — might attract alternative tenants or a sale-leaseback buyer and provide a partial floor, but the timeline and execution risk of any such exit would weigh heavily on recovery valuation.

## The Gap Between Market Pricing and the Dossier's Read

Formal sell-side consensus is thin. TSSI's small-cap status and historically limited float produced sparse institutional coverage before the AI ramp, and while volume and attention increased materially through 2024–2025, the company remained outside the index universes and multi-name programme books that drive consensus formation at larger firms. No published analyst price-target consensus could be independently confirmed as of the frozen-snapshot date.

What the market appears to be pricing at $12 is essentially the base case layered with a liquidity and concentration discount. The dossier's reading is incrementally more constructive on two dimensions the current price does not fully reflect. First, the minimum monthly payment commitments embedded in the December 2025 contract extension provide a partial revenue floor through November 2027 that materially reduces the probability of a sudden zero-revenue cliff outcome. Second, the Georgetown facility's 15 MW committed power allocation — with a development roadmap toward 40 MW — represents a real infrastructure asset that retains optionality for alternative customers or a capital event in a market where purpose-built data centre capacity remains acutely constrained.

Neither factor alone justifies a dramatic re-rating. Together, they suggest the bear case is somewhat less binary than the concentration discount implies. The honest counter is that the stock has already compressed 62% from its peak. The multiple paid at $31.94 reflected peak excitement and extrapolation of 172% revenue growth; $12.00 may prove to be the market's more considered answer to a genuinely difficult question about what a one-customer AI integrator is worth when the contract eventually comes up for renewal.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through the AI integration ramp
chapters.body:
## From the Margins to the Mainstream: Establishing the Baseline

For most of its history, TSS, Inc. operated comfortably below the radar — a specialist in data-centre-services maintenance, systems integration, and what management called its Facilities segment, generating modestly growing revenue from a client base that valued competence over scale. In fiscal year 2022, the company booked roughly $30.6 million in total revenue. By December 2023, that figure had risen to $54.4 million, a 78% increase the company attributed to traction across its procurement and integration practices, as well as investments in personnel and facility layout that shrank rack-completion cycle times. Net income for 2023 came in at just $74,000 — barely above breakeven — on adjusted EBITDA of $2.65 million.

At the close of that fiscal year, Darryll Dewan, the company's president and chief executive officer, struck a tone of deliberate optimism.

> "2023 was a transformational year for TSS. We grew revenues 78% in 2023 and increased our operating income by 91% compared to 2022, while making operational and go-to-market investments in the business. As generative AI, cybersecurity and other advanced computing technologies drive data center demand, TSS is uniquely positioned to capitalize on these trends with our leading-edge system integration and deployment capabilities."

It read, at the time, as aspirational language from a small-cap chief executive. Within twelve months, the numbers would make it look prophetic.

## The Transition Quarters: Q1 and Q2 2024

First-quarter 2024 revenue of $15.9 million — up 142% year-over-year from $6.6 million — arrived on the back of higher procurement activity rather than any AI-programme revenue, which had not yet materialised at scale. Adjusted EBITDA recovered from a $436,000 loss in Q1 2023 to a positive $475,000. The company was still small-cap micro-cap in character: thinly covered, lightly traded, listed on ~~OTC Markets~~ ==the OTCQB Marketplace==.

The second quarter of 2024 presented a curious optical anomaly. Total revenue of $12.2 million fell below Q2 2023's $14.5 million as procurement volumes were lumpy and pulled back from an elevated prior-year comparable. The headline appeared to show contraction. Underneath it, however, the margin structure told a different story: gross profit climbed 41% to $4.5 million and net income surged 345% to $1.4 million, as the company rotated toward higher-yielding systems integration work. In June 2024, TSS expanded its production capacity at its existing Texas integration facility and began integrating AI-enabled server racks for the first time. Dewan was explicit about what was driving the capital outlay:

> "During Q2, we made a significant investment in our production capacity, which came online at the beginning of June. This expansion, compounded with process improvements, has significantly increased our volume capacity for rack integration and decreased the cycle time to complete each rack within our existing facility. The expansion was driven primarily by the surge in demand for server rack builds related to generative AI, as the AI market expands as a whole."

He signalled, with unusual candour for an investor call at a company his size, that the volume trajectory was already in motion:

> "To be clear, the volume ramp we've been anticipating is now underway. Our OEM customers have robust pipelines and we are seeing their deals beginning to close including one significant program that was started in the second quarter and will more dramatically impact the third quarter. We believe our Q2 performance was a harbinger of results to come."

## Breakthrough: Q3 2024 and the Nasdaq Uplisting

The third quarter of 2024 was the period when the story shifted from strategic potential to verifiable inflection. TSS reported revenue of $70.1 million — an increase of 689% over the $9.0 million recorded in Q3 2023 — with net income of $2.6 million, up 1,166% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $4.3 million, up 358%. Procurement services accounted for the bulk of the revenue surge at $60.5 million, growing more than 1,000% on the comparable quarter, while systems integration delivered $7.6 million, up 361%.

Dewan described the quarter's significance in unambiguous terms:

> "We are pleased to report a dramatic increase in earnings in the third quarter, both sequentially and year-over-year. This is the first quarter that includes a full period of revenue for AI-enabled server rack integrations at meaningful volumes."

The same week as the earnings release, TSS completed its uplisting from ~~OTC Markets~~ ==the OTCQB Marketplace== to the Nasdaq Capital Market, a move Dewan explicitly connected to the company's elevated profile: *"We have also elevated our market presence by transitioning from the OTC Markets to the Nasdaq Capital Market today."* Trading volumes and analyst attention followed. On guidance, Dewan maintained that the run-rate was durable: *"We expect results through the first half of 2025 to be similar to our second and third quarters of 2024."*

## Q4 2024 and the Multi-Year Agreement

Fourth-quarter 2024 revenue was $50.0 million, up 105% year-over-year, with systems integration growing 264% to $7.9 million — its strongest quarterly contribution yet as a percentage of the mix. Full-year 2024 revenue reached $148.1 million, up 172% from $54.4 million in 2023, on net income of $6.0 million (versus $74,000 the prior year) and adjusted EBITDA of $10.2 million, an increase of 283%. Operating cash flow came to $15.3 million.

| Segment | FY 2024 Revenue | FY 2023 Revenue | Growth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Procurement Services | $117.5M | $38.5M | +205% |
| Systems Integration | $22.6M | $8.8M | +157% |
| Facilities Management | $8.0M | $7.1M | +13% |
| **Total** | **$148.1M** | **$54.4M** | **+172%** |

The structural underpinning of the fourth quarter was an agreement signed in October 2024 with the company's largest OEM customer — a multi-year contract for AI-enabled rack integration services at an expected minimum monthly volume. The agreement simultaneously formalised the revenue that had driven the Q3 explosion and provided forward visibility for the Georgetown facility investment that management was already planning.

> "2024 was a transformative year by all accounts, driven by strong operational execution… The outlook for our industry is robust with significant capital investment flowing into AI-enabling technologies."

## 2025: Georgetown Goes Live, and a Quarter of Friction

The first quarter of 2025 produced TSS's largest single-period revenue to date: $99.0 million, up 523% year-over-year from $15.9 million in Q1 2024, on net income of $3.0 million and adjusted EBITDA of $5.2 million. Procurement services surged to $90.2 million (+676%) as the OEM programme intensified before the facility transition. Systems integration contributed $7.5 million (+253%).

On May 7, 2025, TSS began initial production at its new Georgetown, Texas integration facility — a 213,000 square-foot building that more than doubled its prior operating footprint. Power infrastructure at the site was originally scoped at 4.5 megawatts, revised upward to 6 megawatts, and then committed at 15 megawatts in the near term, with a long-term roadmap targeting more than 40 megawatts. Capital investment was targeted at $25 million to $30 million, with landlord tenant-improvement allowances funding a portion. Dewan positioned the facility as a differentiated asset:

> "In light of the demanding and rapidly advancing AI computing environment, our new facility is a strong differentiator."

Second-quarter 2025 revenue came in at $44.0 million, up 262% from $12.2 million in Q2 2024, with the Georgetown site reaching full operational status across all capabilities. Systems integration reached $9.5 million. Adjusted EBITDA improved 103% year-over-year. Management raised its full-year 2025 adjusted EBITDA guidance from a minimum 50% increase to a minimum 75% increase versus 2024.

The third quarter introduced an unexpected disruption: revenue of $41.9 million was lower than management had anticipated, as TSS encountered unforeseen operational requirements in the systems integration business related to new facility ramp protocols. New procedures were implemented and management indicated that fourth-quarter rack volumes had improved dramatically.

The fourth quarter of 2025 delivered the acceleration management had flagged. Revenue was $60.9 million, up 22% year-over-year; net income reached $12.2 million (+536%), producing diluted earnings per share of $0.41; and adjusted EBITDA was $7.9 million (+132%). Systems integration contributed $14.2 million (+79%), its highest quarterly absolute level.

| Period | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA | Net Income |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | $54.4M | $2.7M | $74K |
| FY 2024 | $148.1M | $10.2M | $6.0M |
| FY 2025 | $245.7M | $18.6M | $15.1M |

## The Ledger at Year-End 2025 and the Road Ahead

Full-year 2025 revenue was $245.7 million, up 66% from $148.1 million. Net income was $15.1 million, up 153%, and diluted earnings per share of $0.56 compared with $0.24 in 2024. In November 2025, TSS amended and extended its integration agreement with its largest OEM customer by two additional years, effective November 1, 2025. Revenue concentration remained acute: the single largest customer accounted for 99% of 2025 revenue.

Dewan closed the year with language that left little ambiguity about his expectation for the next leg:

> "Our business, providing high-performance computing solutions to global leaders in the AI and cloud infrastructure ecosystem, is scaling profitably. Our largest partner anticipates doubling its AI infrastructure business in 2026 compared to last year."

For 2026, management guided adjusted EBITDA in the range of $20 million to $22 million, with rack integration volumes expected to double versus 2025. A conservative supply-chain posture was baked into the forecast given component availability volatility. Procurement and Facilities Management were modelled to grow more modestly relative to the systems integration trajectory — a composition shift that pointed toward TSS gradually re-weighting toward its highest-margin business even as the company maintained the procurement engine that had provided the revenue scale in 2024 and the first half of 2025.

---

**Sources:** [TSS IR — FY 2024 Full Year Results](https://ir.tssiusa.com/tss-revenue-grows-172-to-a-record-148-1-million-in-fy-2024-increases-eps-to-0-24-up-from-0-00-in-2023/) · [TSS Inc FY2025 Full Year Results — Stock Titan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-k1c2lrh4twml.html) · [TSS Q3 2024 Earnings — Stock Titan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-inc-reports-third-quarter-revenue-of-70-1-million-up-i08tolc1kqad.html) · [TSS Q2 2024 Earnings — Stock Titan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-inc-reports-strong-second-quarter-2024-i05znmpe9f30.html) · [TSS Q1 2025 Earnings — Stock Titan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/TSSI/tss-reports-first-quarter-2025-revenue-of-99-0-million-up-523-eps-of-ipsf3m7go5vq.html) · [TSS Q4 2024 Earnings Call — Investing.com transcript](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-tss-inc-q4-2024-sees-revenue-surge-stock-dips-93CH-3953383) · [TSS FY2023 Results — Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/tss-inc-reports-fourth-quarter-200000663.html) · [SEC EDGAR — TSSI 10-K FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1320760/000165495425004295/tssi_10k.htm) · [SEC EDGAR — TSSI 10-K FY2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1320760/000143774924009879/tssi20231231_10k.htm)

chapters.title: Darryll Dewan, Danny Chism, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Architect: Darryll Dewan's Path from Dell to Georgetown

Darryll Dewan arrived at TSS, Inc. on November 14, 2022, two months before generative AI would become a household conversation and nearly a year before the company's investors could fully appreciate why a 74-year-old veteran of IBM, Amdahl, and a decade at Dell Technologies might be exactly the right person to run a ~~Round Rock~~ ==Georgetown, Texas== rack-integrator. His appointment was low-key by design. TSS was then a thinly staffed, sub-scale data center services provider with a modular data center product line and a procurement reselling business — a company measured in single-digit millions of revenue, not the eight-figure AI integration contracts that would follow.

Dewan's curriculum vitae reads like a genealogy of enterprise infrastructure sales. He graduated from the University of Notre Dame with a degree in economics, then spent his early career at IBM and Amdahl before cycling through i2 Technologies, VA Software Solutions, and Credant Technologies — the endpoint-security firm that Dell acquired in 2012. That acquisition brought him inside Dell's orbit for ten years, where he ran global sales for Dell Endpoint Data Security. The resume detail that matters most to understanding TSS's trajectory, however, is less about what Dewan did at Dell than about who he brought with him afterward.

## Building the Bench: A C-Suite Shaped by the OEM Ecosystem

The executive team that Dewan assembled bears the unmistakable imprint of a deliberate talent strategy. Karl T. Marrott joined as Senior Vice President of Operations eighteen days before Dewan signed his own employment agreement — on November 2, 2022 — and was promoted to Chief Operating Officer effective July 1, 2024, just as AI rack integration volume was accelerating hard. Marrott, 60, brought supply-chain execution depth from Flex, Solectron, and Moduslink, companies that built their reputations on high-volume electronics manufacturing and configuration services. His institutional knowledge of the physical integration workflow — how to sequence labor, manage test throughput, and handle BOM complexity at speed — became load-bearing as TSS's Georgetown facility began handling GPU server racks at hyperscaler scale.

The CFO seat was filled more than eighteen months after Dewan took the helm. Daniel M. Chism, 58, began employment on June 7, 2024, an appointment timed — whether by design or fortunate coincidence — to coincide almost exactly with the revenue inflection that would make FY2025 a breakout year. Chism trained at Ernst & Young, took his Master of Professional Accounting and BBA from the University of Texas at Austin, and holds both the CPA and Chartered Global Management Accountant designations. His operational CFO experience ran through EZCORP, the publicly traded consumer-finance company, and Goodwill Industries of Central Texas — backgrounds that reflect comfort with high-transaction-volume operations rather than capital-markets sophistication. For a company whose finance function needed to scale from small-cap irrelevance to meaningful Nasdaq reporting obligations almost overnight, that profile was arguably the right fit.

The remaining C-suite is strikingly Dell-centric. David Hull, the Chief Technology Officer, spent approximately 29 years at Dell Technologies as Senior Director and CTO for Technology Strategy. Matt Wallace, the Chief Strategy Officer, logged 13 years at Dell culminating as VP, Corporate Strategy and Market Intelligence, after early career stints at Booz & Company; he holds an MBA from UT McCombs. Janet Morrison, the Chief People Officer, brings two decades of HR experience at Ford, Nike, and Dell. That three of four functional C-suite executives share a Dell career history is not incidental: it reflects a conscious effort to embed the operating language, process discipline, and — critically — the relationship capital of the company's anchor OEM customer directly into TSS's leadership layer.

## The Board: Five Seats and a Turnaround Chairman

The TSS board is compact by public-company standards. Five directors sit in three staggered classes, with Dewan occupying the sole non-independent seat. The four independent directors bring a range of backgrounds, but the common thread running through the board's construction is micro-cap infrastructure and logistics expertise, leavened by a late addition whose biography reads as a near-direct signal about the company's strategic direction.

Peter H. Woodward, 53, has served as non-executive Chairman since January 2012 — predating Dewan by nearly eleven years and representing the institutional memory of the long turnaround through which TSS passed before the AI ramp began. Woodward is the founder and president of MHW Capital Management, a New York-based micro-cap focused investment firm. As of the April 2026 record date, MHW entities controlled 2,134,282 shares (7.40%), with Woodward personally holding an additional 219,358 shares for a combined beneficial ownership of 8.10%. He also chairs Precision Optics Corporation on Nasdaq and serves as CEO of Innovative Power LLC. His decade-plus grip on the Chairman seat, combined with control of both independent committee agendas, places him as the dominant governance force at the company.

Richard M. Metzler, 73, brings logistics operating credentials: former CEO of Lone Star Overnight, former CEO of APL Logistics, former EVP at DHL, and currently chairman of Diverse Logistics & Distribution. Michael Fahy, 51, added to the board in October 2024, is CEO and President of Neovia Logistics, a 100-site global contract logistics firm, and previously held regional CEO roles at DB Schenker Americas. The [2026 DEF 14A](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1320760/000114036126016374/ny20068614x1_def14a.htm) contains a governance disclosure that deserves specific attention: it notes that Fahy has "significant business dealings with our largest customer" — a reference to Dell Technologies, TSS's anchor OEM — and records that the board has determined those dealings do not impair his independence under Nasdaq rules. Whether that determination holds up to sustained scrutiny as the Dell relationship grows in revenue materiality is a question that will follow this board into 2026 and beyond.

The most revealing board addition is Dr. Vivek Mohindra, 57, appointed in November 2025. Mohindra served as SVP and Chief Strategy Officer at Dell Technologies from 2020 through 2025, before a brief stint as Special Advisor to Dell's Vice Chair and COO through April 2026. Prior to Dell, he was a general partner at New Science Ventures and an operating partner at TPG Capital. He holds a BE from IIT Roorkee and MS, PhD, and MBA degrees from MIT. His appointment to the TSS board — arriving while his Dell advisory role was still active — reads as an intentional deepening of the relationship between TSS and its anchor OEM customer. His 2025 director compensation consisted of a prorated cash retainer of $6,667 and $101,880 in option awards on joining.

The board operates two formal committees — Audit and Compensation — with no separate Nominating or Governance committee. Woodward chairs both, earning an incremental $15,000 as Chairman and an additional $10,000 as Audit Committee Chair for total 2025 cash fees of $65,000. The Audit Committee met seven times in 2025; the Compensation Committee convened once.

## Pay, Equity, and the AI Ramp Premium

The compensation trajectory of the three named executive officers traces the company's revenue inflection with unusual clarity. Dewan's total Summary Compensation Table figure rose from $593,630 in 2023 to $892,543 in 2024 to $3,081,505 in 2025, a fivefold increase over two years driven almost entirely by stock-award grants rather than salary movement. His 2025 base was $385,000, rising to $400,000 effective January 14, 2026. Chism's 2025 SCT total reached $2,335,233 on a $325,000 base; Marrott recorded $2,289,657 on $300,000 cash.

| Executive | 2023 SCT Total | 2024 SCT Total | 2025 SCT Total | 2025 Base |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|---------------|-----------|
| Darryll Dewan, CEO | $593,630 | $892,543 | $3,081,505 | $385,000 |
| Karl Marrott, COO | $532,094 | $975,652 | $2,289,657 | $300,000 |
| Daniel Chism, CFO | — | $828,988 (partial) | $2,335,233 | $325,000 |

In each case, equity components — restricted stock grants valued at prevailing share prices — accounted for roughly 80% of reported 2025 compensation. At December 31, 2025, at a closing price of $7.07 per share, Marrott held 363,334 unvested restricted shares (market value approximately $2.6 million), Dewan held 355,000 (approximately $2.5 million), and Chism held 267,500 (approximately $1.9 million). The grants vest over time, binding management's accumulated wealth directly to the AI ramp's durability.

## Insider Transactions: Monetization at Scale

No insider purchases of TSS common stock appear in Form 4 filings over the twenty-four months through May 2026. All recorded open-market activity is on the sell side.

Dewan executed sales pursuant to a 10b5-1 trading plan adopted December 15, 2025, selling 50,000 shares at $15 in April, 50,000 at $16 later that month, and 50,000 at $17 in early May 2026 — aggregate proceeds of approximately $2.4 million. Chism sold 25,000 shares at $15 on April 14, 2026 ($375,000), having previously sold 30,000 shares in August and September 2025 at prices around $16.20 for an additional ~$486,000. Marrott sold 39,649 shares across three April 2026 transactions at prices between $15.00 and $15.11, realizing approximately $598,000, on top of similar-scale 2025 dispositions. Senior Vice President Kieran Brennan sold 12,000 shares at $12.27 in March 2026, following a 5,000-share sale at $13.50 in May 2025. Chairman Woodward trimmed 51,700 shares across December 2025 and January 2026 transactions at prices between $8.30 and $8.82.

The uniform absence of purchases belongs in the record without editorial inflation. Executives holding unvested restricted stock and out-of-the-money options at the company's pre-ramp lows have limited rational need to acquire additional shares in the open market. Dewan's plan adoption in December 2025, at prices below those at which his subsequent sales executed, reflects textbook pre-planned diversification. Residual unvested exposure across the three NEOs still exceeds $7 million at the December 31, 2025 reference price — a figure that aligns management's forward incentives with continued execution through the Georgetown ramp.

## Governance in Context

The board's design — small, logistics-and-infrastructure literate, anchored by a long-tenured turnaround chairman with material equity, and now supplemented by a former Dell chief strategy officer — is coherent for a company whose strategic identity is inseparable from a single OEM relationship. It is also a board that concentrates governance authority narrowly: Woodward chairs both independent committees, the nominating function is absorbed rather than formalized, and the Fahy disclosure introduces a relational layer that the proxy handles with a one-sentence independence determination. As TSS's revenue scale and market capitalization grow, the pressure to expand committee differentiation and board independence breadth will grow with them. That is a 2027 governance conversation rather than a 2026 crisis — but it is already visible in the filings.

---
